advances: The actual dyadic depth threshold holds for the entire stated class with a finite convex nondecreasing separable penalty. The proof uses the original fiber-volume law. Sign symmetry reduces ambient caps to continuous-coordinate marginal caps. An ordinary marginal centerpoint handles the regime of continuous dimension at most a fixed constant times the integer dimension. One-coordinate halving tails, common energy tilts, and an inward cube fit of the actual mean handle the complementary regime. This is a structural class theorem and does not resolve the locked problem for arbitrary convex bodies.

proof:
First verify the body and the probability law. Convexity and \(\psi(0)=0\) imply \(\psi(t)\le t\psi(1)\) for \(0\le t\le1\). Hence \(\psi\) is continuous at zero; finiteness and convexity give continuity at every positive argument. They also imply \(\psi(t)\ge t\psi(1)\) for \(t\ge1\). Thus \(\psi\) is continuous and coercive. Each \(x\mapsto\psi(|x_i|)\) is convex, since \(\psi\) is convex and nondecreasing.

For row \(l\), the lower endpoint is \(-R+\sum_i(1+B_{li})\psi(|x_i|)\), a convex function, and the upper endpoint is \(R-\sum_i(1-B_{li})\psi(|x_i|)\), a concave function. Their epigraph and hypograph constraints, and the convex base constraint, prove that \(C_B\) is convex. All constraints are closed. The base constraint bounds every \(|x_i|\) by coercivity. Writing \(E(x)=\sum_iV_i(x)\), the coefficient bounds give \(|c_B(x)_l|\le E(x)\), so every point of the body has \(|y_l|\le E(x)+a(x)=R\). This proves boundedness and compactness. Every constraint is strict at \((0_n,0_d)\), and continuity supplies an ambient open neighborhood in \(C_B\). The body is full-dimensional.

For every point of the base the displayed fiber is the actual nonempty cube. At \(E(x)=R\) it is a singleton. Therefore exactly the fibers in \(D_+\) have positive \(d\)-volume, and that volume is \(w_z=(2a_z)^d\). The support \(D_+\) is finite and contains \(0_n\), whose volume is \((2R)^d>0\). The locked mixed-volume formula proves \(W=\mathcal H_d(S_B)>0\).

Let \(Z\) have the original law \(p\), let \(U\) be independently uniform on \([-1/2,1/2]^d\), and put \(Y=BV(Z)+2a_ZU\). Conditional on \(Z=z\), the variable \(Y\) is uniform on the actual positive fiber. Consequently, for every measurable ambient set \(A\), its original probability is \(\mathbb P((Z,Y)\in A)=\mathcal H_d(S_B\cap A)/W\). No root-weight or auxiliary probability law replaces this identity.

We first record a sign-symmetry reduction that avoids controlling the fourth moment of a full ambient projection. The joint law of \((Z,Y)\) is invariant under \(Z\mapsto-Z\), while \(Y\) is unchanged. Let \(y^\star\in[-R,R]^d=C_{B,0_n}\). For any \(\alpha\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R^d\), the two indicators at \(Z\) and \(-Z\) satisfy

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf1_{\{\alpha\cdot Z+\beta\cdot(Y-y^\star)\ge0\}}
+\mathbf1_{\{-\alpha\cdot Z+\beta\cdot(Y-y^\star)\ge0\}}\\
&\hspace{35mm}\ge
\mathbf1_{\{\beta\cdot(Y-y^\star)\ge0\}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]

Indeed, if the last scalar is nonnegative, at least one of the two preceding scalars is nonnegative. Taking expectations and using invariance proves that every closed ambient halfspace through \((0_n,y^\star)\) has probability at least half the probability of its parallel \(Y\)-marginal halfspace through \(y^\star\). When \(\beta=0\), the latter probability is one. A closed halfspace containing the point contains its parallel halfspace through the point, so the same lower bound applies to all containing halfspaces.

For completeness, the ordinary centerpoint statement used here follows from finite-dimensional Helly's theorem and compactness, and both ingredients have an elementary proof in this setting. For a probability measure supported on the compact cube \([-R,R]^d\), consider all closed halfspaces of measure strictly greater than \(d/(d+1)\), together with that cube. Every subfamily of at most \(d+1\) of these sets has a nonempty intersection: the union of the complements of the halfspaces has measure less than one, including when the cube is one of the sets. Finite Helly gives nonempty intersection for every finite subfamily; compactness of the cube gives a point in their entire intersection.

Here is the finite Helly argument. Any \(d+2\) points have an affine dependence whose coefficients sum to zero. Separating positive from negative coefficients and normalizing them gives a common point of the convex hulls of two disjoint groups. If \(d+2\) convex sets have all their \((d+1)\)-fold intersections nonempty, choose a point in the intersection omitting each individual set. Apply the preceding affine-dependence partition to these \(d+2\) points. For each convex set, one side of the partition contains only points in that set; the common convex-hull point therefore belongs to every set. This proves the case of \(d+2\) sets. Induction on the number of sets, replacing two sets by their intersection, proves the finite theorem, since a \((d+1)\)-fold intersection in the new family is an intersection of at most \(d+2\) original sets.

The \(Y\)-marginal is absolutely continuous, being a finite mixture of uniform positive cubes. If a closed halfspace containing the intersection point had measure less than \(1/(d+1)\), its open complement would have measure greater than \(d/(d+1)\). Moving its boundary a sufficiently small positive distance into that complement would give a closed halfspace still having measure greater than \(d/(d+1)\), but excluding the point. This contradicts the construction. Thus the marginal point has depth at least \(1/(d+1)\). It lies in the origin cube. By (1), an actual point of \(S_B\) has ambient depth at least \(W/[2(d+1)]\). This assertion holds for every \(n,d,\psi,R,B\) in the statement.

We next derive the moments needed only for an inward fit when \(d\) is large. Write \(V=V(Z)\) and \(E=\sum_iV_i\). For each real \(k>0\) and real \(\theta\), define a temporary law on exactly \(D_+\) with probabilities proportional to \(a_z^k e^{\theta E(z)}\); denote its expectations by \(\mathbb E_{k,\theta}\). The original law is exactly the case \(k=d,\theta=0\).

Halve one integer coordinate toward zero. More precisely, let \(T_i z\) replace \(z_i\) by \(\operatorname{sgn}(z_i)\lfloor|z_i|/2\rfloor\), leaving all other coordinates fixed. Convexity and monotonicity give \(\psi(\lfloor m/2\rfloor)\le\psi(m)/2\) for every integer \(m\ge0\). The energy decrease \(\Delta=E(z)-E(T_i z)\) is therefore at least \(V_i(z)/2\). Also \(a_{T_i z}=a_z+\Delta\le R\), and \(T_i z\in D_+\). Each image has at most three preimages: zero has preimages \(0,\pm1\) in that coordinate, and a nonzero coordinate has at most two preimages of the same sign.

If \(\theta\le k/(2R)\), the unnormalized weight ratio obeys

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{a_z^ke^{\theta E(z)}}{a_{T_i z}^ke^{\theta E(T_i z)}}
&=k\log\left(1-\frac{\Delta}{a_{T_i z}}\right)+\theta\Delta\\
&\le-\frac{k\Delta}{R}+\theta\Delta
\le-\frac{kV_i(z)}{4R}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

The logarithm is well defined because \(a_z>0\); the inequality uses \(\log(1-t)\le-t\). Summing (2) over the preimages proves \(\mathbb P_{k,\theta}(V_i\ge t)\le3e^{-kt/(4R)}\) for \(t>0\). Integrating the tail gives

\[
\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_i^2\le\frac{96R^2}{k^2},
\qquad
\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_i^4\le\frac{18432R^4}{k^4}
\quad\left(\theta\le\frac{k}{2R}\right).
\tag{3}
\]

Indeed, for integer \(r>0\) the same computation gives
\(\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_i^r\le3r!(4R/k)^r\).

Under every one of these common-tilt laws, distinct energy coordinates have nonpositive covariance. To prove this, assume \(n\ge2\) and condition on \(V_i=t\). The remaining total energy \(s=\sum_{j\ne i}V_j\) has weights equal to its nonnegative counting multiplicity times \(e^{\theta s}(R-t-s)^k\), on \(s<R-t\). This description permits arbitrary energy gaps and repeated energy values. For two attainable values \(t_2>t_1\), the ratio of the two unnormalized remaining-total weights, up to a constant independent of \(s\), is \([(R-t_2-s)_+/(R-t_1-s)]^k\). It is nonincreasing in \(s\), including the part where it is zero. The conditional mean of \(s\) is therefore nonincreasing in \(t\). One elementary verification is the identity \(2\operatorname{Cov}(f(A),g(A))=\mathbb E[(f(A)-f(A'))(g(A)-g(A'))]\) for independent copies \(A,A'\); oppositely monotone functions give nonpositive covariance. Apply it first to the likelihood ratio and \(s\).

Exchangeability of the remaining coordinates gives \(\mathbb E_{k,\theta}[V_j\mid V_i=t]=\mathbb E_{k,\theta}[s\mid V_i=t]/(n-1)\). A second application of the same covariance identity proves \(\operatorname{Cov}_{k,\theta}(V_i,V_j)\le0\). Consequently,
\(\operatorname{Var}_{k,\theta}E\le n\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_1^2\).
Moreover, exchangeability makes the covariance matrix have diagonal \(v\) and a common off-diagonal value \(\gamma\le0\). Its nonnegative eigenvalues are \(v-\gamma\) and \(v+(n-1)\gamma\), so \(v-\gamma\le n v/(n-1)\le2\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_1^2\). When \(n=1\), the same upper bound is immediate. Thus, in every dimension,

\[
\lambda_{\max}(\operatorname{Cov}_{k,\theta}V)
\le2\mathbb E_{k,\theta}V_1^2 .
\tag{4}
\]

The common tilts also control the centered fourth moment of the total energy, without any log-concavity assertion about its irregularly spaced energy values. Set \(v_0=96nR^2/k^2\), \(t_0=k/(2R)\), and \(E_0=\mathbb E_{k,0}E\). The second derivative of the logarithmic moment generating function of \(E-E_0\) is \(\operatorname{Var}_{k,\theta}E\le v_0\) for \(|\theta|\le t_0\), by (3). Its value and first derivative vanish at zero, so that logarithmic moment generating function is at most \(v_0\theta^2/2\) on this interval. Chernoff's inequality, choosing \(|\theta|=\min\{t/v_0,t_0\}\) for each tail, gives

\[
\mathbb P_{k,0}(|E-E_0|\ge t)
\le2\exp\left(-\min\left\{\frac{t^2}{2v_0},\frac{t_0t}{2}\right\}\right)
\quad(t>0).
\tag{5}
\]

For \(t\le v_0t_0\) the quadratic choice gives the first exponent. For \(t\ge v_0t_0\), the endpoint choice has exponent at most \(-t_0t/2\). These two ranges justify (5) exactly.

Use \(e^{-\min\{a,b\}}\le e^{-a}+e^{-b}\) and integrate \(4t^3\) times (5). The integrals \(\int_0^\infty t^3e^{-t^2/(2v_0)}\,dt=2v_0^2\) and \(\int_0^\infty t^3e^{-t_0t/2}\,dt=6(2/t_0)^4\) yield

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{k,0}|E-E_0|^4
&\le16v_0^2+48(2/t_0)^4\\
&=\left(147456n^2+12288\right)\frac{R^4}{k^4}
\le159744n^2\frac{R^4}{k^4}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

We need the centered fourth moment in arbitrary directions of the energy vector. Here is the exchangeability calculation, included to cover this step independently. For \(n\ge4\), write \(m_4=\mathbb E_{k,0}V_1^4\), \(m_{31}=\mathbb E_{k,0}V_1^3V_2\), \(m_{22}=\mathbb E_{k,0}V_1^2V_2^2\), \(m_{211}=\mathbb E_{k,0}V_1^2V_2V_3\), and \(m_{1111}=\mathbb E_{k,0}V_1V_2V_3V_4\). All these are between zero and \(m_4\), by the weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and exchangeability. If \(\sum_i h_i=0\), put \(A_2=\sum_i h_i^2\) and \(A_4=\sum_i h_i^4\). Expanding the fourth power gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{k,0}(h\cdot V)^4
={}&A_4(m_4-4m_{31}-3m_{22}+12m_{211}-6m_{1111})\\
&+A_2^2(3m_{22}-6m_{211}+3m_{1111})
\le38A_2^2m_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

To check the expansion, the sums over ordered distinct indices for the patterns \(31,22,211,1111\) are respectively \(-A_4,A_2^2-A_4,2A_4-A_2^2,3A_2^2-6A_4\), with multipliers \(4,3,6,1\). The absolute coefficient sums in the two parentheses in (7) are \(26\) and \(12\), and \(A_4\le A_2^2\). For \(n\le3\), Hölder directly gives \(\mathbb E(h\cdot V)^4\le\|h\|_1^4m_4\le n^2\|h\|_2^4m_4\le9\|h\|_2^4m_4\), so the bound \(38\|h\|_2^4m_4\) remains valid.

For arbitrary \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), put \(\bar b=n^{-1}\sum_i b_i\) and \(h=b-\bar b\mathbf1_n\). Let \(\mu^{(k)}=\mathbb E_{k,0}V\). Exchangeability gives
\(b\cdot(V-\mu^{(k)})=h\cdot V+\bar b(E-E_0)\).
Also \(\|h\|_2^2\le\|b\|_2^2\) and \(\bar b^4n^2\le\|b\|_2^4\). Combining \((r+s)^4\le8(r^4+s^4)\), (3), (6), and (7), we obtain

\[
\mathbb E_{k,0}[b\cdot(V-\mu^{(k)})]^4
\le6881280\,\frac{R^4}{k^4}\|b\|_2^4 .
\tag{8}
\]

The numerical coefficient is exactly \(8(38\cdot18432+159744)=6881280\).

Return now to the original law \(p\), with \(k=d,\theta=0\), and put \(\mu=\mathbb E_pV\). Sign symmetry gives \(\mathbb EZ=0_n\), and the conditional noise has mean zero, so the actual full mean is \((0_n,B\mu)\). Since \(\sum_i\mu_i=\mathbb E_pE<R\) and \(|(B\mu)_l|\le\sum_i\mu_i\), this point belongs to the origin fiber and is an actual point of \(S_B\).

Assume \(d\ge n\) and \(d^3\ge16K_\star n^2\). Halving all coordinates toward zero defines a map \(T\) with at most \(3^n\) preimages per image. Its energy is at most \(E(z)/2\), so \(a_{Tz}\ge(R+a_z)/2\). If \(a_z<R/23\), then \(a_z/a_{Tz}<1/12\). Comparing actual weights and summing over the preimages therefore gives
\(\mathbb P_p(a_Z<R/23)\le3^n12^{-d}\le4^{-n}\le1/4\).

For each row \(b_l\) of \(B\), one has \(\|b_l\|_2^2\le n\). Equation (8) and the union bound give

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P_p\left(\max_l|b_l\cdot(V-\mu)|>R/46\right)
&\le d\,46^4\cdot6881280\,\frac{n^2}{d^4}\\
&=K_\star\frac{n^2}{d^3}\le\frac1{16}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

Equations (3) and (4), and \(\|B\|_F^2\le dn\), also give
\(\mathbb E_p\|B(V-\mu)\|_2^2\le192(n/d)R^2\le192R^2\).
Markov's inequality thus gives
\(\mathbb P_p(\|B(V-\mu)\|_2^2>3072R^2)\le1/16\).
The intersection of these three good events has original probability at least \(5/8\). On this intersection the normalized offset
\(\delta_z=(B\mu-BV(z))/(2a_z)\)
satisfies \(\|\delta_z\|_\infty\le1/4\) and
\(\|\delta_z\|_2^2\le3072\cdot23^2/4=406272=L_\star^2\).
Thus the original mean is an inward point of every cube in this event.

We now prove the dimension-independent cube-cap bound used for those fibers. If \(U\) is uniform on \([-1/2,1/2]^d\), \(\|\delta\|_\infty\le1/4\), and \(\|\delta\|_2\le L_\star\), then for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\),
\(\mathbb P(v\cdot(U-\delta)\ge0)\ge\kappa\).

Let \(M(t)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{tu}\,du\), and let \(m(t)=M'(t)/M(t)\). This is the mean of the tilted one-dimensional uniform law. It is continuous, odd, and strictly increasing because its derivative is the strictly positive tilted variance. For \(t>0\), direct integration gives \(m(t)=\tfrac12\coth(t/2)-1/t\); hence \(m(4)>1/4\). Thus, for each coordinate \(\delta_i\in[-1/4,1/4]\), there is a unique \(\theta_i\in[-4,4]\) with \(m(\theta_i)=\delta_i\).

For \(|t|\le4\), the tilted density is at least \(e^{-4}\) on \([-1/2,1/2]\), since \(e^{tu}\ge e^{-2}\) and \(M(t)\le e^2\). Its variance is therefore at least \(e^{-4}\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}(u-m(t))^2\,du\ge e^{-4}/12\). Integrating \(m'(t)\ge e^{-4}/12\) between zero and \(\theta_i\) proves \(|\theta_i|\le12e^4|\delta_i|\).

Let \(Q\) be the product of these tilted uniform laws, and let \(P\) denote the original uniform cube law. Under \(Q\), the coordinates \(U_i-\delta_i\) are independent and centered, have variance at least \(\nu=e^{-4}/12\), and have absolute value at most one. Their fourth central moments are at most their variances, hence at most \(\nu^{-1}\) times the squares of their variances. Expanding the fourth moment of their independent centered linear combination \(F=v\cdot(U-\delta)\) gives
\(\mathbb E_QF^4\le12e^4(\mathbb E_QF^2)^2\).
Its variance is positive.

For any centered scalar variable of positive variance \(\sigma^2\) and fourth moment at most \(J\sigma^4\), Hölder gives \(\mathbb E|F|\ge\sigma/\sqrt J\). Centering gives \(\mathbb EF_+=\mathbb E|F|/2\); Cauchy-Schwarz gives \((\mathbb EF_+)^2\le\mathbb P(F>0)\sigma^2\). Therefore \(\mathbb P(F\ge0)\ge1/(4J)\). Applied under \(Q\), this yields \(Q(F\ge0)\ge1/(48e^4)\).

To transfer this cap probability, the density \(D=dQ/dP\) has
\(\mathbb E_PD^2=\prod_i M(2\theta_i)/M(\theta_i)^2\).
Jensen gives \(M(t)\ge1\). The convex chord bound for \(e^{tu}\) gives \(M(t)\le\cosh(t/2)\le e^{t^2/8}\); the last inequality follows directly from \((2j)!\ge2^jj!\) in the power series. Consequently \(\mathbb E_PD^2\le\exp(\|\theta\|_2^2/2)\le\exp(72e^8\|\delta\|_2^2)\). Cauchy-Schwarz on the cap \(A=\{F\ge0\}\) gives \(Q(A)^2\le P(A)\mathbb E_PD^2\), proving

\[
P(A)\ge\frac1{2304e^8}
\exp(-72e^8\|\delta\|_2^2)\ge\kappa .
\tag{10}
\]

This proves the cube-cap assertion with all dimension dependence removed.

On every good fiber, (10) applies to the marginal cap \(\{\beta\cdot(Y-B\mu)\ge0\}\) for every nonzero \(\beta\). The original good-fiber mass is at least \(5/8\), so each such marginal cap has probability at least \(5\kappa/8\). If \(\beta=0\), its probability is one. Formula (1) now proves that every ambient closed halfspace containing the fixed actual mean has original probability at least \(5\kappa/16\ge\kappa/4\). Thus the first depth assertion holds in the high-dimensional regime.

Finally suppose this regime fails. If \(d<n\), then \(d+1\le n\). Otherwise \(d^3<16K_\star n^2\), which implies \(d<16K_\star n\), since \(16K_\star\ge1\) and \(n\ge1\). In either case \(d+1\le(16K_\star+1)n\). The marginal centerpoint already constructed therefore gives

\[
\frac{h_{S_B}(\mathbf y^\star)}W
\ge\frac1{2(d+1)}
\ge\frac1{2(16K_\star+1)n}
\ge\frac{2^{-n}}{16K_\star+1}.
\tag{11}
\]

The last inequality uses \(2^n\ge2n\) for all positive integers \(n\), proved by induction from \(n=1\). In the high-dimensional regime, the lower bound \(\kappa/4\) is at least \(c2^{-n}\); in the complementary regime, (11) is at least \(c2^{-n}\). The constant \(c\) is strictly positive and less than \(1/e\), because \(\kappa/4<1/(9216e^8)<1/e\). Every chosen point is legal and fixed before the halfspace, and every probability has been transferred through the original actual-volume identity. This proves the theorem for the whole specified class.
statement:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(R>0\), and let \(\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) be finite, convex, and nondecreasing, with \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\psi(1)>0\). Let \(B\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}\) satisfy \(|B_{li}|\le1\). Put \(V(x)=(\psi(|x_1|),\ldots,\psi(|x_n|))^{\mathsf T}\), \(a(x)=R-\sum_iV_i(x)\), and \(c_B(x)=BV(x)\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_B&=\{(x,y):\ \sum_iV_i(x)\le R,\quad
 c_B(x)-a(x)\mathbf1_d\le y\le c_B(x)+a(x)\mathbf1_d\},\\
S_B&=C_B\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d),\\
D_+&=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:\ \sum_iV_i(z)<R\},\qquad
a_z=R-\sum_iV_i(z),\\
C_{B,z}&=c_B(z)+[-a_z,a_z]^d,\qquad
T_z=2a_zI_d,\\
w_z&=(2a_z)^d,\qquad
W=\sum_{z\in D_+}w_z,\qquad p_z=w_z/W .
\end{aligned}
\]

Vector inequalities are coordinatewise. The symbols \(a_z\) and \(w_z\) denote the cube radius and the actual fiber volume, respectively. Thus \(C_{B,z}=c_B(z)+T_z[-1/2,1/2]^d\). In the linear subcase \(\psi(t)=t\), these definitions reduce exactly to the common-cube normalizations with \(V(x)=|x|\). No linear-penalty moment assertion is used as a premise.

The set \(C_B\) is a compact full-dimensional convex body, \(D_+\) is its complete positive integer support, and \(W=\mathcal H_d(S_B)>0\). Its halfspace depth \(h_{S_B}\) has the meaning in the locked problem.

Set

\[
\begin{aligned}
K_\star&=6881280\cdot46^4,\qquad L_\star^2=406272,\\
\kappa&=\frac1{2304e^8}\exp(-72e^8L_\star^2),\\
c&=\min\left\{\frac{\kappa}{4},\frac1{16K_\star+1}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Then \(0<c<1/e\), and for every body in the statement there is one point \(\mathbf y^\star\in S_B\), fixed before the containing halfspace is chosen, with \(h_{S_B}(\mathbf y^\star)\ge c2^{-n}W\).

More precisely, if \(d\ge n\) and \(d^3\ge16K_\star n^2\), the original full mean \(\mathbf y^\star=(0_n,B\mu)\), where \(\mu=\mathbb E_pV(Z)\), satisfies \(h_{S_B}(\mathbf y^\star)\ge(\kappa/4)W\). In the complementary regime a continuous-coordinate marginal centerpoint supplies a point with \(h_{S_B}(\mathbf y^\star)\ge W/[2(d+1)]\ge(16K_\star+1)^{-1}2^{-n}W\).
